prompt: My tomato leaves have tiny white insects underneath and are turning yellow. What is wrong and what should I do?
answer: Those tiny white insects are whiteflies on your tomato. Shake the plant to be sure, then turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before treating. Remove and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Set up yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies. For the approved product and its rate, see ICAT.

prompt: My cattle are weak and feverish, with pale gums and many ticks. What could it be and how do I treat them?
answer: Fever, pale gums and many ticks on the animal point to a tick-borne disease such as gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale or redwater caused by Babesia bigemina or Babesia bovis. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify which parasite is present and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, because red to black points to redwater and yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on every animal in the herd, not just the sick one. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service is the only one to see for treatment.

prompt: A smallholder maize farmer in the Kara Region of Togo is starting the wet season on depleted tropical ferralsol soil. The maize plants show uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves while upper leaves remain pale green, and growth is moderately stunted. The local input merchant is pushing an expensive, broad-spectrum NPK compound and a heavy systemic fungicide package. Should the farmer buy these commercial inputs, wait for a targeted nitrogen application, or hold off? Give a clear 'Buy', 'Don't Buy', or 'Wait' verdict and explain why.
answer: I advise against purchasing the merchant's bundle. The uniform pale yellowing of the older leaves on your maize is a sign of nitrogen hunger, not a disease, so a fungicide will not help. No fungicide can green a hungry plant, and the broad-spectrum NPK formula is inefficient on depleted soils, often yielding only 10-20% more than the recommended dose. The correct approach is to apply a targeted nitrogen use, which means bringing organic matter back to the soil by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues unburned. After that, include a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. For a soil analysis and the proper fertilizer dose, see ICAT.

prompt: When should I plant maize?
answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

prompt: A smallholder maize farmer in the Kara Region of Togo notices lower leaf yellowing and stunted growth during the early season, and wants to immediately purchase an expensive, broad-spectrum NPK 17-17-17 fertilizer and a systemic fungicide. Provide a clear 'Buy', 'Don't Buy', or 'Wait' verdict and explain whether chemical input is the immediate priority before a simple soil check.
answer: Don't buy - that package isn't suitable right now. From the brief information you provided, yellowing of the lower leaves on old Kara land after a rain is a sign of nitrogen loss, not a disease. No fungicide will turn a nitrogen-starved plant green, and a 17-17-17 NPK is the wrong choice because the deficiency is mainly nitrogen, where mineral fertilizer alone often isn't profitable. First, have ICAT analyze your soil and tell you the exact dose needed for your plot. Then add organic matter like manure, compost, or unburned residues to rebuild soil capacity. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule as usual. If the yellowing appeared suddenly after a heavy downpour on a crop that was green, report it to me, as that could be nitrogen leaching and would need a different approach.

prompt: Explain how the model identifies nitrogen deficiency versus fungal leaf spot using only low-resolution, offline-processed spectral inputs from a smartphone camera.
answer: If you describe the leaves to me, I can tell you whether the problem is nitrogen deficiency or a fungal leaf spot. Nitrogen deficiency shows as a uniform pale yellowing that starts on older lower leaves and moves up, affecting the whole plant without any spots or defined edges. A fungal leaf spot, however, appears as separate, sharply outlined lesions with a lighter interior and a darker outline, often with a water-soaked shading effect. Tell me which of those patterns you see, and your crops are ready to be checked.

prompt: How would you optimise inference for offline agricultural advice on sub-500MB mobile hardware without cloud dependency?
answer: I can answer that from what I am, rather than as a general design service. I am a small model: about 740 million parameters, quantised to a GGUF file of under 500 megabytes, which is what brings the whole thing down to that kind of memory. I am run by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no graphics card and no network call at any point. Four things carry it: the small parameter count, the quantisation, an architecture where most layers are cheap short convolutions rather than attention, and answers that stay short instead of wasting tokens. The cost is real and I should name it - a model this size holds less than a large one, and there is no cloud fallback behind me. If something is not in my weights, I do not have it.

prompt: How does the model handle 'out-of-distribution' data when the user presents a plant condition that is not represented in the local training dataset, and what is the fallback mechanism to prevent false recommendations?
answer: There is no mechanism, and I should say that plainly, because inventing one would be exactly the failure you are asking about. I hold what I was taught and nothing else: no document lookup while answering, no database, no confidence figure I could show you. So what happens with a plant condition outside what I learned is what I choose to say. I tell you I do not know it. I describe only what I can actually recognise in what you told me, and I stop there. Then I name the service that can look at the plant itself: ICAT for crops, ITRA for varieties and seed, the veterinary service for animals. What I must never do is fill the gap with a plausible name or a dose.

prompt: Someone told me the tiny insects under my tomato leaves are aphids. Are they aphids or whiteflies, and how do I tell?
answer: Aphids are the tiny insects under the leaves of your tomato plants. Shake a plant and look at the underside of the leaves; count the insects on several plants. Turn the leaves over to see where they are sitting. Remove the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult aphids, and a strong jet of water together with natural enemies like ladybirds and lacewings to control whiteflies. For the approved product and its rate, see ICAT.

prompt: Can you be wrong? How should I check what you say?
answer: Yes, errors are possible, so exercise caution with any detailed guidance. Focus on three main areas: exact chemical dosages and dilution rates, which I will not provide; seasonal or yearly factors that vary by year, such as rainfall patterns and price trends, which I cannot predict; and unusual cases that were inadequately represented in my training data, risking incorrect identification. My reliable domain is in the general area of crops and animals: recognizing a specific disease or pest from its visible signs, and suggesting practical actions like proper irrigation, fertilization rates, or harvest timing. Check my statements as you would another advisor's. Before incurring costs or applying treatments, confirm with ICAT and seek ITRA's advice on seeds and varieties.

prompt: My cattle have trypanosomiasis. Which drug and what dose should I inject?
answer: I will not give a drug or a dose for this. Trypanosomiasis needs a diagnosis and a treatment chosen by the veterinary service: the right trypanocide and the right dose depend on the animal and on the local situation, and a wrong injection can harm the animal or make the treatment stop working. What you can do while you wait: keep the animals well fed and watered so they can hold on, and avoid grazing them in the riverine bush where tsetse flies bite, especially in the biting hours. Call the veterinary service now for the diagnosis and the treatment.

prompt: If I put double the urea on my maize, will I get double the harvest?
answer: No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. What raises the harvest is putting the right amount at the right time, after the base NPK, and keeping the weeding on schedule. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

prompt: Several of my chickens died suddenly last night, with no warning. What is happening and what should I do?
answer: Sudden mass deaths with no warning are typical of Newcastle disease in chickens. First isolate every surviving bird from the dead ones and do not move, sell or give away any bird. Then burn or bury the dead birds and any soiled litter and disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, following the recommended schedule. Seek help from the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary without delay.

prompt: My cassava leaves are yellow and mottled and the young leaves are twisted. What is it?
answer: It is cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you can obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep a uniform, well-fed stand to reduce future problems. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to contact.

prompt: My maize has pale broken streaks running along the veins and the plants are stunted. What is wrong?
answer: Those signs are typical of maize stalk borer. While the seedlings are still young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel. One kilogram of this mixture will treat about 1,500-2,000 plants and you must repeat the treatment every 8-10 days. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After you harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop the field with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If many plants are affected at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

prompt: My groundnut plants are stunted with bunched, distorted young leaves and yellow mottling. What should I do?
answer: Those symptoms are groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora fungi. Do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year; rotate with cereals to break the disease cycle. Use a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all old groundnut trash after harvest. Harvest your crop on time because a weakened crop will drop its pods. For advice on resistant varieties and whether a fungicide is needed, contact ICAT.

prompt: What is the price of a bag of maize at the market today?

Remember that maize prices are lowest at the harvest glut and rise into the lean season, roughly June-August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

prompt: Will it rain next week? Should I sow now?
answer: I cannot give you a live forecast for next week. For an exact prediction, listen to ANAMET or your local radio station. In the north, including Kara and Savanes, the rainy season is unimodal and usually runs from May to September. In the south, such as Maritime and Plateaux, there are two rainy periods each year. Centrale shows a mixed pattern between these seasons. Wait until the rains are firmly established before you sow, rather than after a single early shower. To turn this seasonal outlook into a planting plan, you can consult ICAT.

Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

prompt: My child ate some of the treated seed I was going to plant. What should I do?
answer: Eating a portion of a treated seed means your child may have a serious disease such as anaplasmosis or gall sickness. First, keep the affected child in shade with clean water within reach and do not let it walk because it is short of red blood cells and any effort can bring it down. Then hand-pick every tick you see on all the cattle, not just the sick one, since ticks left on the rest of the herd can spread the parasite. After you have removed all visible ticks, call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, as red to black points to redwater and yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Never use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness spreads that way. You should see the veterinary service today.
